label: Two Applications of High-Dimensional Polytopes
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 289 to 310 and showcases how convex polytopes become engines of proof. We preview two destinations: Lovasz's polytope route to the weak perfect graph theorem, and the Brunn-Minkowski inequality used to sort partially ordered sets efficiently, both flowing from one high-dimensional idea.

label: Why Polytopes Prove Theorems
notes: A polytope encodes combinatorial data as the vertices and facets of a high-dimensional convex body. Facet inequalities become valid constraints, integral vertices become discrete objects, and a single geometric duality can settle a question that resists direct combinatorial attack across an entire family of induced subobjects simultaneously.

label: Perfect Graphs and the Stable Set Polytope
notes: A graph is perfect when chromatic number equals clique number on every induced subgraph. The stable set polytope is the convex hull of indicator vectors of independent sets. Perfection is exactly the condition that clique inequalities suffice to describe this polytope completely, so STAB and QSTAB coincide.

label: Antiblockers and Polytope Duality
notes: The antiblocker of a down-closed polytope packages its facet structure into a dual body. Fulkerson's antiblocking theory pairs the clique-constrained polytope of a graph with that of its complement, so a geometric symmetry mirrors the graph-complement symmetry that the perfection property is supposed to respect.

label: The Weak Perfect Graph Theorem
notes: Lovasz proved that a graph is perfect if and only if its complement is perfect. The polytope argument shows the clique inequalities describe the stable set polytope precisely when they do for the complement, converting the combinatorial conjecture into a verified facet description through the antiblocking involution.

label: Reading the Proof Geometrically
notes: Each maximal clique contributes one facet of the stable set polytope, and integrality of all vertices certifies perfection. The high-dimensional polytope thus stores every induced subgraph at once, letting one convex-geometric statement carry the inductive weight that the original combinatorial argument would spread across many cases.

label: Second Application: Brunn-Minkowski
notes: The Brunn-Minkowski inequality states that the n-th root of volume is concave under Minkowski addition of convex bodies. This single high-dimensional volume inequality is the analytic spine of the sorting application that follows, controlling how the cross-sections of an order polytope grow as we move a slicing hyperplane.

label: Volumes, Slabs, and Concavity
notes: Slicing a convex body by parallel hyperplanes produces cross-sectional volumes whose one-over-n-minus-one root is concave in the slice height. Brunn's slab form of the inequality turns this geometric concavity into a quantitative tool for comparing the sizes of the two halves an order polytope is cut into.

label: Sorting a Partial Order
notes: Given a partial order, we want to reach a total order using few comparisons. The information-theoretic target is order of the logarithm of the number of linear extensions; the open question is whether a single well-chosen comparison can always roughly balance that count of consistent orders.

label: The Order Polytope and Balanced Pairs
notes: Linear extensions correspond to a high-dimensional order polytope, and comparing two incomparable elements splits it by a hyperplane. Brunn-Minkowski forces the existence of a pair whose two probabilities lie between roughly a fifth and four fifths, guaranteeing every comparison removes a constant fraction of the remaining extensions.

label: The 1/3-2/3 Conjecture
notes: The balancing argument gives explicit constants and motivates the famous one-third two-thirds conjecture: every non-total finite poset contains an incomparable pair whose comparison is balanced between one third and two thirds. The polytope proof secures a weaker but fully effective constant sufficient for near-optimal sorting.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Two applications, one method: encode combinatorics in a high-dimensional polytope, then exploit either facet duality or volume concavity. Antiblockers delivered the weak perfect graph theorem; Brunn-Minkowski delivered near-optimal sorting of partial orders. Geometry of many dimensions repays the abstraction with decisive, reusable proofs throughout discrete mathematics.
